title: Validate with Zod
idea: Zod lets you describe valid data as a schema, then check untrusted input against it. Bad input becomes a clear 400 before any real work runs.
points: `z.object({ ... })` declares the fields; `z.email()` and `z.string().min(8)` set rules.
`safeParse` never throws. It returns `success` with `data`, or `error`.
`error.issues` lists every problem, each with a `path` and a `message`.
`data` holds only the declared keys. Unknown keys such as `role` are dropped.

walk.text: The schema: a valid email, and a password of at least 8 characters.
`safeParse` checks the body. A missing body is `undefined`, which fails cleanly instead of crashing.
Turn Zod's issues into the API's 400 shape: a `path` string and a `message`.
On failure, answer 400 and stop. Nothing below this line runs.
Use `parsed.data`, not `req.body`. Only validated fields get through.
A stand-in for lecture 7's hash and insert. It counts how often it runs.
Send one good body and three bad ones. Only the good one reaches the insert.

pitfalls: Validate on the server. Client-side checks help users, but anyone can call your API directly.
Read `parsed.data`, not `req.body`. The raw body still holds unchecked extra keys.
`z.email()` checks the format only. It cannot tell whether the mailbox exists.

quiz.why: `safeParse` returns instead of throwing. `n` is too short, so it fails. `extra` is an unknown key, which Zod drops without an issue.

takeaway: Parse input with a schema at the door; use only the parsed result.
